848.title: Plainchant
848.hook: single-line melodies sung for centuries in monasteries: one voice, no harmony, no beat
848.howItsDone: In Catholic monasteries and some cathedrals, the Psalms and parts of the Mass are still sung in Gregorian chant through the day; some Anglican and Lutheran communities sing plainsong too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Margery Kempe, the pilgrim who wept out loud and told her life to a scribe. Your line was tears are allowed. Did anything move you enough to show? Day eight hundred forty-eight.

It's dark outside, well before dawn. In a stone chapel, men in black robes stand in two rows facing each other. Nobody plays an instrument. Nobody keeps a beat. One voice lifts a short phrase, and then the whole row answers on the same notes, in unison, like one long breath shared by everybody. The other row answers back. The melody climbs a little, rests, falls. There's no chorus, no drop, no harmony underneath. Just one line of sound moving through the room, and the words of a psalm riding on it. Today's word is the name for that sound.

Gregorian chant is the old sung prayer of the Latin church, and it goes by other names too: plainchant, or plainsong. It is one melody line, sung by everyone together, with no harmony and no fixed rhythm. The rhythm comes from the words themselves. A long word gets room. A short one moves on. Where does the name Gregory come from? Tradition links it to Pope Gregory the Great, and old paintings show a dove at his ear, as if the Holy Spirit were singing the melodies to him while he wrote them down. Some historians think the chant grew slowly, from many singers in many places, and was gathered under his name later. Either way, the name stuck. The words are often the Psalms. Monks sang them through the hours of the day, from before dawn to nightfall, and the Psalms themselves describe that rhythm. In the King James Bible, Psalm 119 says: "Seven times a day do I praise thee." And the letter to the Ephesians speaks of "psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord." And here's what chant asks of a singer. Nobody stands out. There's no solo star, no harmony part for the good singers. Everyone sings the same note at the same moment, so the voices blur into one. The aim is that the prayer is heard, not the people singing it. Some Catholic monasteries still sing it through the day, and so do some Anglican and Lutheran choirs.

Here's the practice: one line, sung. If you have a recording of plainchant nearby, play it quietly and just listen, letting the line carry you. If you don't, make your own single line. Settle, and breathe in. On the out-breath, hum one low, easy note, as long as the breath lasts. Breathe in again. Hum again, the same note, or one step higher. No tune. No performance. Nobody's listening. Let the note do the work. If you pray, you can let a short line from a psalm ride on the hum. The bell holds the time.
Gregorian chant. Plainsong: one melody line, sung together in unison, with the rhythm of the words, carrying the Psalms through the hours of the day.
Your line: one line, sung. Today, at some ordinary moment, the dishes or the walk home, hum one plain line under your breath, and let that be enough. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

849.title: Erasmus
849.hook: a scholar prints the Greek New Testament and wants the ploughboy singing scripture
849.howItsDone: Christians in many churches study the Bible alongside its Greek and Hebrew, and comparing translations side by side is a common part of Bible study groups and sermon preparation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregorian chant: plainsong, one line of melody carrying the Psalms through the day. Your line was one line, sung. Did you hum it anywhere? Day eight hundred forty-nine.

Proof sheets, the ink still wet, spread across a table in a printer's shop in Basel. A priest is leaning over them, correcting as fast as they come. On each page, two columns. On one side, the New Testament in Greek, the language its writers used. On the other, a fresh Latin translation he has made himself. Readers who had known the gospels all their lives in one familiar Latin wording are about to find a page that lets them check it against the Greek, line by line. Some will be thrilled. Some will be furious. Today: Erasmus.
screen: `GREEK ON ONE SIDE, LATIN ON THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: Desiderius Erasmus was a priest and scholar from Rotterdam who traveled widely, writing letters, editing old books, and poking fun at the church he loved. He belonged to a movement people called humanism, and its rallying cry was two Latin words: ad fontes. To the springs. Back to the sources. Drink the water where it comes out of the rock, not after it has run down a long pipe. For Erasmus, the spring was the Greek of the New Testament, and the early Christian writers who read it. So he gathered Greek manuscripts, compared them, and printed a Greek text beside his own Latin. Where his Latin differed from the familiar wording, readers noticed, and some were alarmed. Why touch what the church had read for so long? His answer, roughly, was that loving the text means looking hard at it. In the preface, a little essay he called the Paraclesis, the exhortation, he says something that still sounds bold. He wishes the scriptures could be read by everyone, women too, and turned into every language. He pictures the farmer singing a piece of it behind the plough, the weaver humming it at the loom, the traveler shortening the road with its stories. Erasmus stayed in the Catholic church all his life. He wanted the church cleaned up from the inside, by learning and by plain imitation of Christ, not torn apart. Soon others would take his Greek text and his questions much further than he ever meant to go. A saying went around that Erasmus laid the egg and Luther hatched it. Erasmus did not enjoy that one.

Here's the practice: read one verse in two translations. Take the angels' song from Luke. The King James Bible says, "on earth peace, good will toward men." The Douay-Rheims, an old Catholic English translation, says, "on earth peace to men of good will." Settle, and breathe. Say each one slowly in your head. Notice where they meet and where they part. Don't decide which is right. Just let the two sit next to each other, the way Erasmus set his two columns side by side. If you pray, you can rest on whichever line speaks to you. The bell holds the time.
Erasmus. A priest and scholar who printed the Greek New Testament beside his own Latin, wanted scripture in every language, and called people back to the sources.
Your line: back to the sources. Today, when you hear a claim secondhand, a quote, a headline, a rumor, go and find where it actually came from before you pass it on. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

850.title: Block close: the middle centuries
850.hook: cathedrals and crusades, mystics and plague, saints and scandals
850.howItsDone: Christians remember the saints of the medieval church on their feast days, and churches have also made public confessions and apologies for wrongs done in Christ's name, including the crusades.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Erasmus, the scholar who set the Greek beside his own Latin and called people back to the springs. Your line was back to the sources. What did you trace back to where it came from? Day eight hundred fifty.

Lay the whole block out on a table, like photos from a long trip. A cathedral floor with a labyrinth set into the stone. A knight's sword raised over a city. Francis bending to kiss a leper's hand. A cart of the dead in a plague year. A monk in a forest leaving bread out for a bear. A pope being scolded in a letter by a young woman from Siena. A man burned for his preaching. A press printing Bibles. Pick up any one photo and it tells you something true. Pick up only one and it lies. Today we close the middle centuries.

This block began at Cluny, with monks praying in shifts so that the prayer never stopped, and with the slow, sad parting of the churches of east and west. It gave us Anselm's faith seeking understanding, Bernard's plain white abbeys, and Hildegard's music. It gave us Francis, Clare and Dominic, and Elizabeth of Hungary with bread in her apron. Aquinas wrote vast books and then called them straw. Dante climbed toward the love that moves the sun. In the east, Gregory Palamas taught stillness and light, and Rublev painted three angels at an open table. Julian spoke through her window, Catherine wrote to a pope, Joan stood trial, and Margery wept. And the same centuries hold the crusades, cities sacked in Christ's name, the burning of Jan Hus, and the plague that emptied whole households. So how do you tell this story? Some tellers keep only the light: the saints and the spires. Others keep only the shadow: the swords and the scandals. Both versions are easier, and both are false. Jesus has a parable about this, a field where wheat and weeds come up together. The servants want to rip the weeds out, and the owner says, in the King James Bible: "Let both grow together until the harvest." And Paul says the treasure is real, but the containers are made of clay: "we have this treasure in earthen vessels." Christians read those lines in more than one way. But they give a way to hold this block: the beauty doesn't cancel the failure, and the failure doesn't cancel the beauty. Next comes a church that knows it needs reform.

Here's the practice: hold beauty and failure together. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person, a group or a place you love that has also let you down. A family, a team, a church, a town, maybe yourself. In one hand, hold one thing about it that's beautiful. In the other, one thing that went wrong. Don't let either hand drop. Don't rush to make them balance. Just hold both and breathe. If you pray, you can offer both hands to God together. The bell holds the time.
Block close. The end of the middle centuries: cathedrals and crusades, mystics and plague, saints and scandals, held in the same hands.
Your line: both are true. Today, when you hear a story told as all good or all bad, a person, a place, a past, ask what the other half looks like. Day eight hundred fifty.

851.title: A church needing reform
851.hook: voices across the church agreed it needed reform; the sale of indulgences became the spark
851.tomorrow: The righteous shall live by faith (Romans 1:17)
851.howItsDone: The Catholic Church still teaches about indulgences and grants them for prayer, pilgrimage and works of charity, never for sale; Protestant churches do not use indulgences, and some Reformed churches use the saying 'always reforming' about themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the middle centuries: cathedrals and crusades, saints and scandals. Your line was both are true. Where did you find the other half of a story? Day eight hundred fifty-one.

A procession comes into a German town square. Banners, candles, a cross, and in the middle, carried with great ceremony, a papal document. A preacher climbs up and begins. Give toward the building of a great church in Rome, he says, and receive a letter of indulgence. For yourself. Even for your mother and father, who have died. People push forward with coins. And a little rhyme starts going around, one that tradition puts in the mouth of a preacher named Tetzel: as soon as the coin in the box rings, a soul out of purgatory springs. A new block begins with today's word.

First, what an indulgence is, in Catholic teaching, because the word is easy to mock and harder to explain. When a sin is confessed and forgiven, Catholics say, its guilt is taken away, but some of its damage can remain, a kind of debt that still needs healing, in this life or in purgatory. An indulgence is the church releasing some of that debt, drawing on the goodness of Christ and the saints, for someone who prays, makes a pilgrimage or does a good work. Giving to the poor or to a church could be one of those works. You can see where it went wrong. A gift became a price. Preachers sold letters from town to town, some promising far more than the church taught, and the money ran to building projects and to people's pockets. The Bible already had a word for buying holy things. In Acts, a man named Simon offers the apostles money for the power of the Spirit, and Peter answers, in the King James Bible: "Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money." Something else belongs in this story. People inside the church were already saying it needed reform: preachers, scholars like Erasmus, bishops, councils, ordinary believers. Catholics would later forbid the selling of indulgences outright, while still teaching what indulgences are. Reformed Protestants later had a saying for the idea in today's line, that the church must always be reformed. And a much later Catholic council, the Second Vatican Council, spoke of the church as always in need of being purified. The disagreement that comes next is real. But the hunger for reform was not only Protestant.

Here's the practice: name one thing in you that needs reform. Not your whole life. One thing. A habit that has slowly turned from a gift into a price. Something you started doing for good reasons that now runs on autopilot, or on fear, or on money. Settle, and breathe. Let it come to mind. Don't punish yourself for it. Just name it plainly, the way you'd name a crack in a wall you mean to fix. If you pray, you can hold it before God. If you don't, hold it in the light for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Indulgence. In Catholic teaching, the church's release from some of the debt that remains after a sin is forgiven. Its sale became the spark for the reformations.
Your line: always reforming. Today, take the one thing you named and change one small part of it, once, before the day ends. Day eight hundred fifty-one.

852.title: The righteous shall live by faith (Romans 1:17)
852.word: The righteous shall live by fait
852.hook: a tormented monk named Luther reads Romans and feels the gates of paradise open
852.howItsDone: Justification by faith is a central theme of Lutheran teaching, and Christians across traditions study Romans together, often reading Paul alongside the prophet he quotes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word indulgence: a gift that became a price, and voices across the church asking for reform. Your line was always reforming. What small thing did you change? Day eight hundred fifty-two.

A friar kneels in confession, and he's been there a long time. He lists his sins. Then he remembers more, and goes back. He fasts, he prays through the night, he follows the rule of his order to the letter, and still he can't shake the feeling that God is a judge waiting to condemn him. His name is Martin Luther. He's a monk, and he teaches the Bible at the university in Wittenberg. Looking back years later, he wrote that one phrase in Paul's letter to the Romans had become hateful to him. Today's line is that verse, and what happened when he read it again.

Here's the verse, in the King James Bible, Romans chapter one: "For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith." As it is written. Paul is quoting the prophet Habakkuk, who says: "the just shall live by his faith." The phrase Luther hated was the righteousness of God. He had been taught to hear it, he says, as God's own justice, the righteousness by which God punishes the unrighteous. And if that is what the gospel reveals, how is it good news? So he kept beating at the verse, his word, until he saw it differently. The righteousness of God here, he came to think, is not what God demands of us but what God gives us. A gift, received by trusting it. The just shall live by faith. In his own telling, he felt as if he had been born again and had walked through open gates into paradise itself. The whole Bible looked different afterward. Christians still disagree about how faith and good works fit together. Lutherans and other Protestants stress that people are made right with God by grace through faith, as a gift. Catholic and Orthodox teaching also says it is all grace, and speaks of faith working through love, growing over a lifetime. In our own time, Catholic and Lutheran churches have signed a joint statement saying they share a basic understanding here, while still differing in emphasis. But the moment in the study belongs to Luther: a frightened man, a single verse, and gates he hadn't known were open.

Here's the practice: read Romans one seventeen, slowly. Settle, and breathe. Say it once in your head: the just shall live by faith. Then again, leaning on the word just. Then again, leaning on live. Then only the last two words: by faith. Notice which word you lean on, and whether it sounds like a demand or a gift today. There's no right answer. Luther kept knocking on it for a long time. If you pray, you can let the line become a prayer as it is. If you don't, just let it sit. The bell holds the time.
The righteous shall live by faith. Paul, quoting Habakkuk, in Romans one seventeen: the verse Luther heard first as a threat, and then as a gift.
screen: `THE RIGHTEOUS SHALL LIVE BY FAITH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the gates opened. Today, when you catch yourself earning or proving, stop once and notice something you've been given instead. Day eight hundred fifty-two.

853.title: Ninety-five theses (1517)
853.hook: Luther posts theses for debate, and printers carry them across Europe
853.howItsDone: Lutheran and other Protestant churches mark Reformation Day at the end of October, remembering the theses; in recent years some Catholic and Lutheran churches have marked it together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Romans one seventeen: the just shall live by faith, and a frightened monk who felt the gates open. Your line was the gates opened. What were you given that you didn't earn? Day eight hundred fifty-three.

Hammer, nail, church door. That's the picture on posters, in films, on coffee mugs: a monk in a black habit nailing a sheet of paper to a wooden door while a crowd gasps. The story goes that Martin Luther did exactly that, at the castle church in Wittenberg, on the eve of All Saints. Historians still argue about the hammer. What isn't in doubt is the paper. It was written in Latin, in numbered points, and its title called it a disputation. In other words, it was an invitation to argue. Today: the ninety-five theses.

A thesis, in a university then, was a statement put up for debate. Scholars would post a list, and anyone could come and argue the other side. So Luther's theses were not a manifesto. They were questions, sharpened into claims, about the indulgence preaching we met two days ago. Luther preached in his town as well as teaching, and people from that town were coming back with indulgence letters and asking whether they still needed to change their lives. That bothered him. So the very first thesis goes straight to the words Jesus begins preaching with in Matthew. In the King James Bible: "Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." When Jesus said repent, Luther writes, he meant the whole life of a believer to be repentance. Not one payment. A whole life of turning. Further down, the questions get sharper. Near the end, Luther passes on questions he says ordinary people were asking. One goes, roughly: why does the pope, who is very rich, not build his great church in Rome with his own money instead of the money of poor believers? And here's the surprise. The theses don't yet throw out indulgences. They ask what indulgences can and can't do, and they say ordinary people deserve honest answers. Luther also sent them, with a letter, to his archbishop. Then something happened that he hadn't planned. Printers got hold of them, translated them out of Latin, and they ran across Germany and beyond far faster than any debate could be arranged. A list meant for scholars became a conversation for everyone. Christians have argued ever since about what that conversation broke and what it opened. But it began as a question.

Here's the practice: write one honest question down. Settle, and breathe. Let a question come up that you've been carrying but not asking. About faith, about work, about someone you love, about yourself. Not an accusation. A real question you'd like an honest answer to. When it comes, find a scrap of paper or your phone and write it down in one sentence. Then sit with it written there, outside your head. You don't have to post it anywhere. If you pray, you can bring the question to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Ninety-five theses. Luther's numbered claims for debate about indulgences, written in Latin for scholars, and carried by printers to everyone.
Your line: a question for debate. Today, ask your honest question of one person you trust, and then listen to their side all the way through. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

854.title: Worms (1521)
854.hook: before the emperor, Luther refuses to recant unless shown wrong by scripture and reason
854.howItsDone: Lutherans and other Protestants remember Worms as a stand for conscience and scripture; Catholic and Lutheran churches today discuss this history together in their official dialogues.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ninety-five theses: numbered questions for debate that printers carried everywhere. Your line was a question for debate. Who heard your question, and did you hear their side? Day eight hundred fifty-four.

A hall packed with princes, bishops and knights. At the front, on a raised seat, the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles. On a table in the middle, a pile of books. A monk in a plain habit is brought in and stood before them. An official points at the books and asks two questions. Are these yours? And will you take back what's in them? He says yes to the first. To the second, he asks for time. He's given one night. The city is called Worms, and the meeting is an imperial assembly. Today: Worms.
screen: `A PILE OF BOOKS ON A TABLE.`

segments.voice: The next day Luther came back and gave his answer, first in German, then again in Latin. Some of his books, he said, were about plain Christian faith, and even his opponents agreed with them. How could he take those back? Others attacked abuses. Others attacked people. He admitted he'd sometimes been harsher than a monk should be. But recant? Unless he was convinced by the testimony of scripture or by clear reason, he said, he could not and would not. His conscience was captive to the word of God, and to go against conscience was neither safe nor right. Early printed accounts add the line people remember: here I stand, I can do no other. Whether he said those exact words, historians aren't sure. The idea isn't new. When the apostles were ordered to stop preaching, Peter answered, in the King James Bible: "We ought to obey God rather than men." The next day, the emperor answered with his own statement of conscience. He would hold to the faith of his forebears, he said, and stake his kingdoms, his friends and his life on it. Two men, each sure of his conscience, each staking his life. Luther was declared an outlaw. Christians today read Worms in different ways. Protestants often see a man standing for scripture against power. Catholics may see a monk breaking with the church's teaching authority, and an emperor keeping faith. What both sides can recognize is a person refusing to say what he didn't believe, with the whole room watching.

Here's the practice: stand by your conscience, kindly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you won't say or do, even when it would be easier. Something you hold to, quietly. Now picture someone who sees it differently. Remember that the emperor spoke of his conscience too, and allow that they may be standing by theirs. Hold both. Firm, and kind. If you pray, you can ask for courage and gentleness together, in your own words or a line you already know. The bell holds the time.
Worms. The German city where Luther, before the emperor, refused to recant unless shown wrong by scripture and clear reason.
Your line: here I stand. Today, if you're asked to say something you don't believe, decline it in plain words, give your reason, and leave out the contempt. Day eight hundred fifty-four.

options: yes, all of it, to keep the peace.
no, unless shown wrong by scripture or clear reason.
nothing; you walk out of the hall.
fork.reveal: he would not recant unless convinced by scripture or clear reason, because his conscience was captive to the word of God.

trapdoor: what you thought: here I stand, a famous quote.
what it means: Luther refused to recant unless shown wrong by scripture and clear reason, and the emperor answered with his own conscience.
what a scholar hears: an imperial assembly, a speech given in Latin and German, and a famous line found in early printed accounts that may not be his exact words.
